newsitem.title: KENYA: Victorious Zaire rebels target mineral-rich Shaba.
newsitem.headline: Victorious Zaire rebels target mineral-rich Shaba.

text.p: Rebels who have captured Zaire's third largest city of Kisangani are now targeting mineral-rich Shaba region where scared government troops are retreating, a regional military source said on Sunday.

The source, who closely monitors Africa's latest war between rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) and Zaire's ragged and mercenary-backed army, said the rebel advance through Shaba could be much faster given strong anti-government feelings there.

Rebels on Saturday captured Kisangani in the biggest setback to ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko and his government in five months of civil war during which it has lost control of at least one-fifth of the vast country.
Residents said by telephone that rebels swept almost unopposed into the city centre on Saturday after soldiers looted what they could and fled across the Zaire River.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila told a news conference at his headquarters in the eastern city of Goma that his forces did not plan to stop there, a view supported by the military source.
"All signs are that they (rebels) are now targeting Shaba province. This is important for them because of Shaba's strategic importance," the source said.
He said the rebels had to do very little fighting in Shaba because of retreating government troops afraid of the rebel advance and popular anger against them by residents.
The source gave an example of the lakeside town of Pweto, which government troops abandoned on Saturday and the town of Manono captured a few weeks ago.
"In both cases not a single shot was fired by rebels. The local population rose up against government gendarmes in the two towns and the rebels made a heroic entry," the source added.

If confirmed, the fall of Pweto would put the rebels within 400 km (250 miles) of the Shaba capital Lubumbashi and could signal the start of a rapid march by Kabila's rebels through the region, regional analyst said.

Senior military and security officials observing the Zaire conflict in neighbouring Zambia said on Saturday they had detected backward movements by Zairean soldiers too scared to face a rebel assault.

The Zambians confirmed the departure of government troops from Pweto and said their intelligence pointed to a "mood of panic" by troops in other towns, most of which share a land or water border with Zambia.
Shaba is home to Zaire's huge copper and cobalt deposits and a hotbed of opposition against ailing and absent President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Military analysts say the advance in Shaba is backed by exiled Zairean Katangese rebels flown home by the Angolan government to join in the fight to overthrow Mobutu.

The Angolan government has denied involvement in the Zaire conflict but diplomats monitoring the war say the Katangese fighters have been flown to Kabila's territory from bases around the Angolan capital Luanda.

The Katangese rebels fought failed secessionist wars in Zaire's southern Shaba province against Mobutu in the 1960s and 1970s. Many left for Angola after they were defeated, where some joined the military.

Western diplomats in Luanda say a number of senior Angolan government officials, while outwardly denying any involvement in the Zairean conflict, were supporting the rebels who have been fighting in the east of the country since October last year.
They wanted an opportunity to strike back at Mobutu for his support of forces opposed to the Angolan government.
